front: What happened to sport and society during the Industrial Revolution?
back: Sport transformed from popular recreation into more organised 'rational recreation' as society became urbanised and industrialised.
group: Rational recreation

front: What were the key characteristics of rational recreation?
back: Organised, with complex written rules, regionally/nationally standardised, more respectable, less violent, and with regular fixture lists.
group: Rational recreation

front: What factors caused the change from popular to rational recreation?
back: Urbanisation, industrialisation, improved transport (railways), increased free time, factory legislation, and the influence of public schools.
group: Rational recreation

front: How did improved transport affect sport in this period?
back: The expansion of the railways allowed teams and spectators to travel further, enabling regional and national competitions and leagues.
group: Rational recreation

front: What effect did the Factory Acts have on sport?
back: Reduced working hours, such as a Saturday half-day, gave the working classes more free time to participate in and watch sport.
group: Rational recreation

front: What role did the public schools play in the development of modern sport?
back: They codified rules, promoted 'athleticism' and used sport to build character, leadership and discipline.
group: Public school athleticism

front: What is 'athleticism'?
back: The Victorian public school philosophy that combined physical endeavour with moral integrity.
group: Public school athleticism

front: What is 'muscular Christianity'?
back: The belief that participation in sport builds moral and physical strength, linking Christian values with physical activity.
group: Public school athleticism

front: Who were 'melancholic' and 'cavalier' headmasters?
back: Melancholic headmasters banned popular recreation activities in schools; cavalier headmasters turned a blind eye, allowing them to continue.
group: Public school athleticism

front: What role did Thomas Arnold play in the development of school sport?
back: As headmaster of Rugby School, he used sport to instil discipline, leadership and moral values (athleticism) in pupils.
group: Public school athleticism

front: What was the significance of public school 'old boys' in spreading sport?
back: They took organised sports and games to university and wider society, forming clubs and national governing bodies.
group: Public school athleticism

front: What was the amateur/professional divide in Victorian sport?
back: Amateurs, typically upper/middle class, played for enjoyment without payment; professionals, typically working class, were paid to play.
group: Public school athleticism

front: What were National Governing Bodies (NGBs) and why were they formed?
back: Organisations formed to standardise rules and administer a sport nationally, e.g. the Football Association, founded in 1863.
group: Public school athleticism

front: Why did football split into rugby and association codes?
back: Disagreements over handling the ball and hacking led public schools and clubs to form separate governing bodies (the FA in 1863, the RFU in 1871).
group: Public school athleticism

front: How did the Church lose control of the population?
back: Migration of people from villages to cities meant it became harder to control large populations
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: How did the Church promote sport and recreation in the late 19th century?
back: The Church encouraged social control, civilised activities and provided facilities for sport
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: Why did the Church support rational recreation?
back: To encourage social control, promote Christian values and civilise working-class leisure time
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: What happened as a result of more people attending church?
back: Behaviour started to improve
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: How did the middle class emerge in the 19th century?
back: Urbanisation and industrialisation led to the rise of self-made entrepreneurs and professionals
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: What was the middle class concerned about?
back: Philanthropy and improving working-class welfare
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: What two laws were introduced to improve working conditions and recreation?
back: Factory Acts – Limited working hours, giving workers more free time for leisure; Municipal Reform Act – Improved urban living conditions and access to public spaces
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: What did the middle class do to increase general health and how did this benefit them?
back: Built facilities such as swimming baths and local parks; Healthier workers could work harder and for longer

front: What was an amateur?
back: Someone who paid to play the sport

front: What was codification? (Impact of the middle class)
back: The combining of different rules of the same sport to create one universal sport with specific rules; dominated by the middle class

front: How did competitions help develop sport? (Impact of the middle class)
back: Matches between different teams of the same social class gradually developed into leagues and national competitions
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: How did public provision help develop sport? (Impact of the middle class)
back: Facilities such as swimming baths improved the quality of life and sporting opportunities for the working class

front: How did English public schools contribute to the spread of sport?
back: They promoted the games ethic, teaching moral values through structured sport

front: What was the purpose of sport within the British Empire?
back: To instil discipline, fair play and social control, helping bind people within the Empire
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: How did young educated men influence sport globally?
back: They became leaders, teachers, missionaries, diplomats and military officers, spreading British sport throughout the Empire
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: How did British sport become international?
back: English rules and structures (e.g. football, rugby and cricket) were adopted worldwide, standardising sport

front: What did schoolboys also develop?
back: National Governing Bodies (NGBs)

front: What led to the formation of National Governing Bodies (NGBs)?
back: The increasing popularity of sport, the formation of more teams and clubs, and the need for organised competitions

front: How did NGBs help structure sport?
back: They organised national and international fixtures, ensuring structured leagues and competitions

front: Why was codification important in sport?
back: Different teams and schools played different versions of sports, so NGBs created nationally agreed rules for fair competition
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: How did NGBs attempt to control professionalism?
back: They maintained the amateur ideal to resist professionalism and retain control over sport

front: What was popular recreation?
back: Unorganised sport and pastimes; e.g. mob football

front: What was rational recreation?
back: Organised sport with formal rules and structure

front: Who played a key role in developing the Wenlock Olympian Games?
back: Dr. William Penny Brookes, a doctor and surgeon who was passionate about physical education

front: Identify two aims of the Wenlock Olympian Games.
back: To improve the body and its abilities; To form an Olympic class

back: The Wenlock Olympian Society, formalising the event structure

front: How did Dr. Brookes contribute to PE in schools?
back: He campaigned for physical education to be included in the school curriculum

front: What was the Industrial Revolution?
back: The movement from farming to factory working
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: What were some impacts of the Industrial Revolution during the first half of the nineteenth century?
back: Migration of the lower classes into urban areas; Loss of space to play traditional mob games; Lack of leisure time due to long working days (6 days a week); Low income; Poor health; Loss of rights through changes in criminal law affecting mob games and blood sports; Lack of public provision
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: What were some impacts of the Industrial Revolution during the second half of the nineteenth century?
back: Improved health and hygiene; Gradual increase in wages and more leisure time for sport; Emergence of a new middle class; Influence of ex-public school boys; Growth of athleticism; Industrial patronage; Improvements in transport and communication; Cheaper travel
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: What were the problems and solutions that came with urbanisation?
back: Lack of space → Municipal Acts; Large working-class populations → Education became compulsory; Loss of traditional sports → Factory Acts; Changes in working conditions → More free time and increased wages
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: What were the characteristics of the transport revolution?
back: Movement of teams and spectators; Improved access to different parts of the country; Cheaper train travel; Improved access to the countryside
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: How did education improve for the working class in the second half of the nineteenth century?
back: Education gradually improved, leading to better reading and writing skills
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: How did increased literacy impact communication?
back: Newspapers became more widely read, improving communication and awareness of events
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: How did improved education influence sport?
back: More people could read about sport, leading to increased interest and participation
group: Impact and characteristic on assossiation football, lawn tennis, Wenlock olympic games

front: What role did newspapers play in sport?
back: They helped create sporting heroes and role models, inspiring future generations
